to basic rulemaking documents—could facilitate a far more deliberative 
and engaged mode of public interaction with agency rulemaking processes. 
See, e.g., Beth Simone Noveck, The Future of Citizen Participation in the 
Electronic State, 1ISJLP 1 (2004/2005). See also Peter M. Shane, Turning 
GOLD into EPG: Lessons from Low-Tech Democratic Experimentalism for 
Electronic Rulemaking and Other Ventures in Cyberdemocracy, 1 ISJLP 
147 (2004/2005). On the other hand, there are clear potential barriers to 
realizing this ideal scenario. On the pubhc input “supply side,” it is by no 
means obvious that the skills, resources, and motivation to participate 
effectively in agency rulemaking proceedings are sufficiently widespread 
for electronic rulemaking to produce a dehberative process significantly 
more inclusive or better informed. See Cynthia R. Farina, Dmitry Epstein, 
Josiah Heidt, & Mary J. Newhart, Knowledge in the People: Rethinking 
'‘Value'' in Public Rulemaking Participation, 41 WAKE FOREST L. Re v . 
1185, 1217 (2012); Cynthia R. Farina et al.. Rulemaking 2.0, 65 MIAMI L. 
Re v . 395, 395 (2011). On the “demand side,” it is equally uncertain whether 
agencies are eager or equipped to engage effectively with a more open 
process. See Peter M. Shane, Empowering the Collaborative Citizen in the 
Administrative State: A Case Study of the Federal Communications 
Commission, 65 MIAMI L. Re v . 483—505 (2011).
The most obvious challenge for agencies that succeed in ehciting a 
much higher volume and intensity of pubhc involvement in administrative 
rulemaking is what to do with all the input. Professor RusseU Weaver has 
noted the trend:
With the advent of the internet, the number of comments 
submitted has risen dramatically, often creeping into the 
hundreds of thousands, sometimes in the milhons. When the 
Federal Communications Commission (FCC) conducted a 
rulemaking on net neutrahty in 2014, it received some 3.9 milhon 
comments. That number was dwarfed by the number of comments 
received (22 milhon) when the FCC requested public comments on 
whether to repeal the net neutrality requirement. As an FCC 
spokesman stated, there is an obvious “tension between having an 
open process where it’s easy to comment and preventing 
questionable comments from being filed, and, generally speaking, 
this agency has erred on the side of openness.”
RusseU Weaver, Rulemaking In An Internet Era: Dealing With Bots, Trolls 
& “Form Letters," 21 Ge o . Ma sON L. Re v . 553, 560-61 (2020). This 
phenomenon looms especiaUy large for agencies because, as we have seen 
in the cases highlighted in this chapter, an agency’s failure to take note of 
and respond to significant issues raised during the public comment period 
can put its rule in legal jeopardy.
